stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office due to a 1-week history of low-grade fever, malaise, sore throat, and persistent nonproductive cough.  Medical history is unremarkable and the patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs.  Temperature is 38.4 C (101 F), blood pressure is 118/75 mm Hg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 22/min.  Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.  Physical examination shows mild pharyngeal erythema, no nasal congestion, and widespread, faint, end-inspiratory crackles.  Chest x-ray shows bilateral, patchy, interstitial infiltrates.  Sputum Gram stain shows numerous leukocytes but no organisms.  Which of the following agents is the best initial treatment for this patient?​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌

options.text: Inhibitor of bacterial cell wall synthesis

explanation:
Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Respiratory droplet transmission
  • Incubation 2-3 weeks
  • Outbreaks in close contacts (eg, school, military)

Clinical presentation

  • Mild, gradual illness; scattered crackles & wheezes
  • CBC: hemolytic anemia, normal/mildly increased WBCs
  • CXR: patchy reticulonodular/interstitial infiltrate

Treatment

  • Macrolides (eg, azithromycin), doxycycline
  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone (eg, levofloxacin)

CBC = complete blood count; WBCs = white blood cells; CXR = chest x-ray

This patient has atypical pneumonia, presenting with low-grade fever, nonproductive cough, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest x-ray.  In a young, otherwise healthy patient, the most common cause of atypical pneumonia is Mycoplasma pneumoniae (or Chlamydia pneumoniae).  These pathogens typically cause mild symptoms, with patients often presenting in the ambulatory setting (ie, walking pneumonia).

Unlike typical organisms that cause lobar pneumonia (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae), M pneumoniae and C pneumoniae lack a classic peptidoglycan cell wall.  M pneumoniae has no cell wall, while C pneumoniae has an atypical cell wall with a unique peptidoglycan component.  Therefore, these pathogens cannot be seen on Gram stain (which stains peptidoglycan) and cannot be treated with antibacterial agents that target peptidoglycan such as penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, or carbapenems (Choice B).

Treatment options for uncomplicated atypical pneumonia include bacterial protein synthesis inhibitors, such as macrolides (eg, azithromycin) and doxycycline.  Respiratory fluoroquinolones (eg, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are also effective.  Legionella pneumophila, another common cause of atypical pneumonia, can also be treated with azithromycin or levofloxacin.  However, this pathogen is usually associated with gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, diarrhea), more severe clinical illness (eg, high fever).

(Choice A)  Trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole are antagonists of folate synthesis; they are ineffective in treating M pneumoniae, which does not synthesize folate de novo.  They are the first-line therapy for Pneumocystis pneumonia, which can also manifest with a bilateral patchy infiltrate and subacute symptoms but typically occurs in patients who are immunocompromised (eg, due to AIDS or chronic glucocorticoid therapy) and causes significant hypoxemia.

(Choice D)  Azole medications (eg, fluconazole) inhibit the synthesis of ergosterol, a primary component of the cell membrane of fungi.  Fungal pneumonias occur most often in the setting of immunosuppression and are uncommon in healthy young patients.  They also are often associated with lobar, nodular, or cavitary infiltrates.

(Choice E)  Mycolic acid is found in the cell wall of mycobacteria (eg, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex) and can be targeted by mycolic acid synthesis inhibitors (eg, isoniazid).  Mycobacteria typically produce more severe chronic symptoms (eg, weeks of productive cough) and constitutional findings (eg, weight loss) with distinct x-ray findings (eg, upper lobe cavitary infiltrates).

Educational objective:Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a leading cause of atypical pneumonia.  Because this pathogen lacks a cell wall, it is not visible on Gram stain and cannot be treated with beta-lactam antibiotics.  Protein synthesis inhibitors (eg, macrolides, tetracyclines) are the treatment of choice.​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌
